style: the teacher reads it herself (Reading Studio), topic-32 scripts (2026-10-14): math_patches/_ai_vis_t32.py is the source - edit there and re-run it. Rules: real_exam/TEACHING_STYLE_GUIDE.md R1-R35 (no 'which way is better' verdict) + NITZAN_RHYTHM_DELIVERY.md P1-P13. Calm preset on the question reading and plain calculations.

slides.say: The rectangle in the accompanying figure is made of forty congruent squares, each with a side of one centimeter. What is the shaded area?
at: The rectangle in the accompanying figure

slides.say: What is the shaded shape? A trapezoid? Let's count its sides. One, two, three, four, five. It's a pentagon, and we never learned an area formula for it. We call these shaded-area questions, and there are two main approaches.

[short pause] One approach takes an area we know, the rectangle, and subtracts the white parts. The other breaks the shaded area into shapes we know, with completions or with symmetry. We'll see all of them. Subtracting is the main one, and the most common, so we start with it.
at: One approach takes an area we know

slides.say: The rectangle has forty squares, so its area is forty. The white parts are four right triangles in the corners, and the area of a right triangle is leg times leg, over two.
Top left: the legs are three and two. Three times two is six, over two is three. Top right: the legs are five and two, so it's five. The two bottom ones have legs of two and three, so three each.

All the white parts together are three plus five plus three plus three, fourteen. Forty minus fourteen is twenty-six. Choice number three is our answer. Careful, fourteen, choice number one, is the white part, not the shaded part.
at: Choice number three is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now completions. Many students count whole squares, and when two pieces of squares complete each other into one whole square, they count them as one.
Here the sloping sides cut squares into odd pieces, so we look at them in groups. Cut the grid into five rectangles: four in the corners, and one in the middle.
at: Cut the grid into five rectangles

slides.say: Look at the top left rectangle, three by two. The sloping side goes from corner to corner, so every shaded piece has a white piece just like it, turned around. They complete each other, so the shaded part is half of six, three.
at: Look at the top left rectangle

slides.say: The same in the other corners: half of ten is five, and half of six is three, twice. The middle rectangle is all shaded, four by three, twelve whole squares. Three plus five plus three plus three plus twelve is twenty-six. Choice number three again.
at: The same in the other corners

slides.say: [pause] And the third way, with the symmetry principle we already know. We break the shape into pieces we know. Draw a line between the two side corners of the pentagon.
Above the line there's a triangle. Its base is the whole width, eight, and its tip is on the top side of an eight by two rectangle. So it's half of sixteen, eight.
Below the line, the middle rectangle is four by three, twelve. And each side triangle is half of a two by three rectangle, half of six, three.

Eight plus twelve plus three plus three is twenty-six. Choice number three again. So in a shaded-area question, subtract the white parts from a shape you know, or break the shaded part into shapes you know. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
